newsitem.title: FRANCE: JOSPIN DEBUT SPEECH AWAITED FOR FRENCH POLICY TIPS.
newsitem.headline: JOSPIN DEBUT SPEECH AWAITED FOR FRENCH POLICY TIPS.

text.p: French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin makes his debut parliamentary speech on Thursday under pressure to deliver on election promises of more jobs and a little less austerity on the road to European monetary union.

The balancing act will be tough for Jospin, who formed a new left-wing government two weeks ago and has spent most of the time since then plunged in negotiations to get employment nudged higher up the European Union agenda.

Jospin is expected to formally announce an audit of public finances, leaving him time to prepare the ground within his "Pink-Red-Green" coalition for a possible mini-budget after the audit is completed around mid-July.

That reappraisal is expected by many to confirm that France will be hard pushed to limit its public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year in line with a strict interpretation of criteria for joining the launch of the euro single currency in 1999.
The finance ministry's budget division was already sending out warnings shortly before the June 1 election, saying the 1997 deficit could lie between 3.4 and 3.8 percent.

Economists believe Jospin will make a showcase speech to the National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, reaffirming a pledge to voters to push for a shorter working week and create 700,000 jobs within three years, half in the public sector.

He is likely to hold up France's securing of an "employment pact" at the EU summit in Amsterdam as the first step in his government's bid to ensure that monetary union does not run roughshod over the bloc's 18 million unemployed.

Some analysts feel he might openly predict that the deficit is likely to overrun three percent of GDP this year, while reaffirming his campaign stance that France can live with this and that monetary union should not hinge on a "decimal point" dogma which is not even prescribed by the Maastricht treaty.

Jospin has a number of other more immediate issues to deal with, notably calls for a significant increase in the national minimum wage, the SMIC, and demands that talks be reopened on wage rises for several million public sector employees.
He may announce a hike in the SMIC, which is currently 6,406 francs per month, amid expectations he will pick a level half-way between union demands for a four to eight percent rise.
He will also be watched for signals that he supports the reopening of public sector wage negotiations.

The previous centre-right government imposed a tight pay increase totalling 2.8 percent over this year and next in the face of vocal opposition from trade unions which are seeking a "catch up" offer to compensate for a pay freeze in 1996.

In line with his promises to boost public sector employment, he also has to decide what to do about the previous government's plan not to refill more than 5,000 civil service posts this year, mostly in the state school system.

Economists believe Jospin could couple a SMIC wage hike with a promise of lower payroll taxes and also a small cut in the value added tax on basic household goods, with the resultant shortfall in social security revenue made up by a rearrangement of other taxes.

On privatisations, most financial market experts believe it is too early for Jospin to announce definitive positions on the sale of stakes in France Telecom or defence electronics group Thomson-CSF -- planned sell-offs which have been on the back-burner since the centre-right was ousted from power.

Another thorny task for Jospin will be deciding the fate of the costly, fault-prone Superphenix fast-breeder nuclear reactor which his Green party environment minister Dominique Voynet has vowed to shut down.
Jospin also plans to convene a "national conference" of employers and trade unions on wages, work time and employment and may confirm union predictions that it should start in September.
